20.0.0.en: Ben-hadad: a common name for the kings of Aram.

20.0.1.en: Aram: they are the origin of the present Syrian people, and they lived between the mountains of Lebanon and the region between the two rivers, that is, Iraq. Many states were named Aram according to the region in which the Arameans lived, so there were Aram of Damascus, Aram of Zobah and Aram of the two rivers; that is, the Arameans lived in a huge region that was divided into many states.

20.0.2.en: For political or economic reasons Ben-hadad king of Aram thought of seizing Samaria and the lands of Israel that belonged to it. So he gathered thirty-two kings who were subject to him, allied with him, and neighboring his country, and set out with a huge army of horses, horsemen and chariots, and besieged Samaria and began to war against it, that is, to aim his weapons at it and hurl his missiles upon it. The city of Samaria was so well fortified that the king of Assyria later had to besiege it for three years until he brought it down and carried the kingdom of Israel into captivity (2 Kgs 17:5).

20.1.0.en: In pride Ben-hadad, who was besieging Samaria, sent messengers to King Ahab, who lived in Samaria, demanding that he hand over all the silver and gold he had, as well as his wives and his children. This means that Ben-hadad had become king over Samaria and what belonged to it. Perhaps Ben-hadad meant by these demands to provoke Ahab to refuse, so that he would have a pretext to attack Samaria and seize it. This shows how confident Ben-hadad was in his huge military power.

20.2.0.en: In humiliation and fear Ahab agreed to all of Ben-hadad's demands. This shows how sin humbled Ahab, and the weakness of Baal, whom he worshiped and relied on, appeared; whereas David the prophet, by the power of God, triumphed over the Arameans and subdued them. Ahab did not remember this, so as to repent and return to God and imitate David. Nor did he remember what Elijah did with him when God's power and Baal's weakness appeared (ch. 18), for his heart was still stony and far from God.

20.2.1.en: Sin humbles man, but when God reigns over the heart, He strengthens man and raises him in glory and splendor. So do not be lax with sin, lest it humble you; and if you sin, the door of repentance is open, that you may regain your sonship and your glory, and Satan will not be able to dominate you.

20.3.0.en: Ben-hadad's messengers returned to him and informed him of Ahab's agreement to his demands, so Ben-hadad grew in pride and greed. He sent his messengers a second time to Ahab, declaring to him that Ben-hadad was not content with his first demands but wanted to send his servants to search the king's palaces and the houses of his servants and subjects, to take from them not only everything precious or whatever Ben-hadad found pleasing, but also everything desirable and great in the eyes of Ahab and his servants, such as the idols they worshiped. He wanted not only the material things Ahab possessed but also to humiliate him. And so we see in Ben-hadad an image of Satan, who cannot be appeased; if we yield to him partially, he goes further to crush and humiliate us.

20.4.0.en: Ahab felt the humiliation increasing upon him, so he called the leaders of the people and its elders and told them how great an evil Ben-hadad wanted to do to him and to them, because he had agreed to his first demands, so Ben-hadad grew in greed and in humiliating him with his second demands. In all this Ahab did not seek God but sought help from people, because he had forgotten God; and on the other hand he did not turn to Baal, because he was sure of his weakness, as appeared in his meeting with Elijah (ch. 18). Ahab called the elders of the people for the following reasons:

20.4.1.en: 1- Because Ben-hadad's demands were not limited to his palace but extended to the houses of the people and its leaders as well.

20.4.2.en: 2- He felt fear at soldiers entering every place in Samaria, and at his being exposed, with all his people, to humiliation and death.

20.5.0.en: The leaders of the people felt how great the humiliation would be that would come upon them all when Ben-hadad's soldiers entered their houses, and they might overstep and kill whomever they wished of them. So they declared to the king their rejection of Ben-hadad's demands, since they preferred death to this humiliation, or they felt that in either case they were exposed to death. Perhaps they relied on the fortification of their city and not on their military strength, because Ben-hadad's power was very great.

20.6.0.en: Ahab answered the messengers who came to him with the second message that he could not accept it, and in humiliation and fear he told them two things:

20.6.1.en: 1- "I am a servant to Ben-hadad", for he said, "Tell my lord Ben-hadad".

20.6.2.en: 2- He confirmed his agreement to the first demands, that he himself would hand over his possessions, his wives and his children, but that no one would search the palaces of Samaria.

20.6.3.en: Perhaps Ahab was encouraged by the opinion of the elders of the people, and so he declared his refusal of the second demands.

20.7.0.en: Ben-hadad was greatly enraged when his messengers returned to him bearing Ahab's refusal of his second demands, so he sent his messengers a third time bearing an extremely violent message of threat, in which he swore by his gods that he would destroy Samaria and make it rubble and dust, and that because of the multitude of his army Samaria would be small before his might, so that if each soldier took a handful of the dust resulting from the destruction of the city, this dust would be less than the number of his soldiers. This shows:

20.7.1.en: 1- His complete confidence in his gods.

20.7.3.en: 3- His contempt for Samaria and its God and all who were in it.

20.7.4.en: And in his oath by the gods his great confidence in them appears, for he said: if I do not destroy Samaria, as I have declared, may the gods destroy my country and add to its ruin beyond what I wish to do to Samaria. He was completely confident that he would destroy Samaria, and of course the gods did not destroy his country, because they are nothing.

20.8.0.en: He that girdeth on: the soldier who puts on his weapons and binds them to his body, such as armor and helmet. He that putteth it off: the soldier who has won the victory and returned to his homeland and taken off his weapons.

20.8.1.en: Since Ahab was strengthened by the encouragement of the leaders of the people, he replied to Ben-hadad's third message, saying: do not boast that you have secured victory over Samaria, for you have not fought and have not won, and you do not know the future, and any unexpected things may happen that hinder your seizing Samaria. In all this Ahab did not return to God, but thought with his own mind and the words of his elders.

20.9.0.en: When Ahab's reply to Ben-hadad's third message arrived, Ben-hadad was immersed in his pleasures, drinking wine with the kings allied with him in this war, and this shows how reckless he and those with him were; they were not attentive with concentration and ready for this war. It also shows that Ben-hadad was given to pleasure, and this is what would lead to his defeat and that of those with him, and it reminds us of King Belshazzar, king of Babylon, who was immersed in drinking wine and his pleasures in the days of Daniel, and how he and those with him died and Babylon fell on that very night (Dan 5). In pride Ben-hadad commanded his army to get ready and take position to attack Samaria, while Ben-hadad himself kept drinking wine with the vassal kings, immersed in his pleasures, which had taken control of him.

20.10.0.en: God's wonderful tenderness toward all mankind, even toward those who disobey Him and defy Him, appears in that He looked upon Ahab, who persisted in idol worship and was humiliated before Ben-hadad, and yet did not return to God. God had compassion on him and sent him a prophet from among the prophets who had been hiding for fear of Ahab and Jezebel, and now he appeared by God's command and relying on God's power, to bring Ahab the good news of what he could not have expected, namely that God would be with him and give him victory over this very great army of Ben-hadad's. Thus God's overwhelming power would be shown, defeating this mighty army by means of the very small army with Ahab, since his military strength had become very weak, only seven thousand soldiers (v. 15). By this good news God intended several things:

20.10.1.en: 1- That Ahab would repent and believe in God and reject the pagan gods that were unable to rescue him from Ben-hadad, and that God alone would rescue him.

20.10.2.en: 2- That the people, led by their elders, would believe in God when they saw Him give them victory and deliver them from Ben-hadad. For if they had not lived by the faith they declared before Elijah when the fire accepted his sacrifice, God would appear in power a second time when He delivers them from Ben-hadad.

20.10.3.en: 3- The breaking of the pride of Ben-hadad and all the kings with him, that God's power might appear above all the pagan gods whom Ben-hadad and those with him worship.

20.10.4.en: 4- That He might show His seeking love toward man who does not seek Him, just as He became incarnate to redeem us, and they crucified Him, then He rose to raise all who believe in Him.

20.10.5.en: God is seeking you and calling you to Him every day, so do not neglect His voice, but thank Him and obey Him, and you will live and rejoice in fellowship with Him.

20.11.0.en: Ahab was strengthened by the good news of this prophet, because he no longer had any support or help except from God, so he submitted to Him and asked the prophet for the details of how this victory would be accomplished. He said to him, "By whom?", that is, who will fight the Arameans; and, strangely, God said to him through the prophet's mouth: "By the young men of the princes of the provinces". For the kingdom of Israel was divided into provinces, that is, governorates or districts, and each province had an administrative head with a special guard, and these were these young men, whose work was guarding and who were not trained to fight against enemies. But God's power is displayed when He works through the weak, so that the power may be God's. And Ahab obeyed because of his weakness and helplessness.

20.11.1.en: Then he asked the prophet a second question: "Who shall order the battle?" Will Israel, or will he wait until the Arameans attack? And God's answer was that Ahab himself should lead the young men of the princes of the provinces and begin by attacking the Arameans, in order to test Ahab's obedience to God and his faith, and to establish this faith when he is victorious, so that perhaps after this he might live with God. But sadly, after the victory he left God and offered Him not even one thank offering, nor did all the people, and he returned to his former life of idol worship.

20.12.0.en: Ahab numbered the young men of the princes of the provinces, and they were two hundred and thirty-two, a very small number to face tens of thousands of the Aramean army. He also numbered the army of the kingdom of Israel that was in Samaria, and they were seven thousand, who would follow the young men of the princes of the provinces. All this was so that God's power might be displayed with His weak people, and when He gives them victory over the Arameans the glory is God's alone.

20.13.0.en: The army of the children of Israel went out, led by the young men of the princes of the provinces, and King Ahab himself led the army. This was at noon, when the army of Aram did not expect war, since war usually begins in the morning. Ben-hadad and the vassal kings were immersed in their pleasures, drinking wine, for Ben-hadad in pride had despised the children of Israel, and this increased his immersion in his pleasures.

20.14.0.en: Ben-hadad learned from his watchmen of the going out of soldiers from Samaria, and perhaps he heard the noise of their going out, so he sent messengers to make sure and learn the truth about those going out from Samaria. His messengers informed him that there were a few soldiers, about three hundred, who had come out of the city and were advancing on the camp of the Arameans. In all pride he commanded that they be taken alive, whether they had come out surrendering to Ben-hadad or had come out for war. This shows:

20.14.1.en: 1- Ben-hadad's pride and his confidence in the strength of his armies, that he could easily take alive any number of the children of Israel and had no need to kill them.

20.14.2.en: 2- His confidence in the weakness of the children of Israel before him, so he would seize those coming out against him, to kill them whenever he wished. Perhaps he wanted to torture them before killing them, to be an example to the people of Israel, to frighten them so that they would surrender to him easily.

20.14.3.en: 3- Ben-hadad wanted to take them alive in order to obtain from them information that would help him in seizing the city.

20.15.0.en: The young men of the princes of the provinces went out from the city of Samaria, followed by the army of the children of Israel, the seven thousand, and God gave them faith and strength, so they attacked the army of the Arameans and each of them killed the man before him. The army of the Arameans was afraid of this sudden attack and the falling of some of them, so the Aramean army fled, and the army of Israel pursued them and killed some of them, and their fear and flight increased, so that their king Ben-hadad was very afraid and shocked at what had happened, and he had no choice but to flee on a horse among the horsemen, in disguise, leaving his royal chariot, to save himself.

20.15.1.en: Then Ahab went out with the seven thousand to pursue those fleeing from the army of Aram, killing as many of them as he could and smashing their chariots, so God made a great slaughter in the army of the Arameans. In this victory we see the following:

20.15.2.en: 1- God gave strength and psychological support to the young men of the princes of the provinces, who were untrained for war, so they attacked with force and killed all whom they met.

20.15.3.en: 2- God put terror in the hearts of the Arameans, so they were afraid and fled at once.

20.15.4.en: 3- Ben-hadad's immersion in drinking wine made him unable to face the situation, so he fled in humiliation and helplessness.

20.15.5.en: 4- This great, unexpected victory ought to have led Ahab to faith in God and to the removal of idol worship, but sadly he did not return to God.

20.16.0.en: Ahab did not send to the prophet of God who had given him the good news of victory, to thank him, but the tender God took the initiative a second time and sent this prophet to Ahab, informing him that Ben-hadad would return to fight him at the turn of the year, probably meaning the summer, when conditions are suitable, since the day is long and there is no rain. So God here warns Ahab to prepare his armies and weapons for war months before it begins. He did not tell him this the first time, because Ben-hadad had already besieged Samaria and there was no time to prepare.

20.16.1.en: Ben-hadad is a type of Satan, who does not cease to fight us however much we triumph over him. Therefore be always ready and do not slacken if you achieve any victory over him and reject his sins. Hold fast to God's commandments, set a guard over your senses, and keep away from what makes you stumble, and you will live victorious all your life.

20.17.0.en: The counselors of the king of Aram thought that the gods of the children of Israel were gods of the hills, which is why they were able to defeat Aram in the hills surrounding Samaria. This was counsel from them that the king had not asked for, but they were eager to offer it for the good of the kingdom.

20.17.1.en: In ancient times they believed that there were gods of the mountains, gods of the valleys and gods of the seas. Because they believed that the children of Israel were like the other peoples and had gods like the gods of the peoples, they thought that the gods of the children of Israel were gods of the hills whose power appeared only on the hills. They thought this belief for the following reasons:

20.17.2.en: 1- The abundance of mountains in the land of the children of Israel.

20.17.3.en: 2- The children of Israel did not use chariots, because they are not fit for war except in the valleys.

20.17.4.en: 3- The people of Israel used to offer their sacrifices on the hills, meaning of course the pagan gods into whose worship the inhabitants of the kingdom of Israel had fallen.

20.17.5.en: 4- Perhaps the Arameans knew that the children of Israel sang to their God psalms that showed that He was a god of hills, as David says, "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills" (Ps 121:1) and "His foundation is in the holy mountains"

20.17.6.en: (Ps 87:1). In addition to this, the huge size of the Aramean army shows in the valleys and not on the hills, and so they would terrify the army of Israel.

20.18.0.en: The counselors gave Ben-hadad counsel for victory over the children of Israel, and their plan included a set of proposals:

20.18.1.en: 1- To fight them in the plain, where there are no hills, so that victory over them would be easy, because of their belief that the gods of Israel were gods of the hills only.

20.18.2.en: 2- To remove the thirty-two kings subject to Ben-hadad and appoint military commanders in their place so that they could lead their armies.

20.18.3.en: 3- To prepare a great army like the first one that besieged Samaria, with the same number of horsemen, soldiers, horses and chariots, that is, in great multitude that would guarantee victory. The king agreed to their counsel and began to carry it out, and this shows the ignorance into which the followers of idol worship fall, for they do not know that there is one God for the whole universe, and He is able to do all things and protects His people Israel.

20.18.4.en: And all the items of the plan show Ben-hadad's pride and his reliance on the multitude of his armies and plans, for he was not humbled even after his defeat.

20.19.0.en: Aphek: a city lying east of the Sea of Galilee, about five kilometers away, in a plain that is higher than the city of Damascus.

20.19.1.en: Ben-hadad carried out the counsel of his servants. At the turn of the year after his attack on Israel he prepared an army like the first and moved toward the city of Aphek, where there was a wide plain, to fight Israel, and he went up to Aphek because Damascus, where Ben-hadad lived, is lower than Aphek.

20.20.0.en: When Israel learned of the movement of the armies of the Arameans and their arrival at Aphek, their army got ready and they took the provisions they needed, because the place was far from Samaria and their cities, since Aphek is considered to be in the north of the land of the Jews. The number of the army of the children of Israel was very small compared with the huge army of the Arameans, and Israel divided its army into two companies, so they looked like two little flocks of kids before the hosts of the Aramean army, for flocks of goats are always small in number. But their reliance was on God's power that supported them, as the prophet had given them the good news (v. 22).

20.21.0.en: To encourage His people Israel, God sent them His prophet for the third time, and called him a man of God, because he is God's voice to His people. The prophet spoke to King Ahab and told him that since the Arameans had thought that the Lord is a God of the hills, and not a God of the valleys, they will see how God gives you victory over them. By this two things are accomplished:

20.21.1.en: 1- Ahab and the people of Israel will know that God has authority over the whole world, so they will believe in Him and abandon idol worship.

20.21.2.en: 2- The Arameans will know that the God of Israel is the only God, above all their gods, so that they may believe in Him.

20.22.0.en: Footmen: a soldier of the infantry and not a horseman.

20.22.1.en: The two armies met at Aphek, but they remained for seven days without either of them moving, for the following reasons:

20.22.2.en: 1- The army of the Arameans was in fear as a result of its first defeat, so it was observing the points of weakness and strength in the army of Israel and drawing up its plans to destroy them.

20.22.3.en: 2- The army of Israel trusted in God's power and awaited His intervention, as He intervened in the days of Jericho, which fell after seven days (Josh 6:15-21). It did not know how it would be victorious, but it trusted in the victory.

20.22.4.en: And after seven days the two armies engaged, and God's power was with His people, so they won a crushing victory over the Arameans and killed a huge number of them, one hundred thousand footmen, which was most of the Aramean army, for the following reasons:

20.22.5.en: 1- The trust of the people of Israel in God's power made them attack the army of the Arameans with force and courage.

20.22.6.en: 2- God cast terror into the hearts of the army of the Arameans, so they tried to defend themselves but in weakness, and so this huge number of them fell.

20.22.7.en: 3- Perhaps the army of the Arameans, in their fear and confusion as they tried to flee, killed one another, as happened with the army of the Midianites in the days of Gideon (Judg 7:22).

20.23.0.en: After the crushing defeat of the army of the Arameans and the death of most of them, only twenty-seven thousand soldiers were left of them, and they all fled to the city of Aphek to take refuge inside its walls. And here God intervenes to give the Arameans their due, who had overstepped against Him and claimed that He was a God of the hills only, so He stretched out His hand and allowed the walls of the city of Aphek, with the buildings connected to them, to fall upon them. Perhaps this was by an earthquake that occurred in that region, and they all died, and so what they tried to take shelter in, the wall, fell on them, for who can stand before God? He alone is the source of protection. As for King Ben-hadad, in his terror he fled from house to house and from room to room, for fear of the buildings falling on him. And what the army of Israel had expected came about, that God would give them victory as He gave victory to His people in the days of Jericho, so the walls fell to kill the rest of the Aramean army. The king was followed by a few of his counselors and servants, who survived the falling of the walls and buildings upon them.

20.24.s.en: (4) Ahab's pardon of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him

20.24.0.en: Sackcloth on our loins: coarse clothing worn on the waist and below, a sign of humbling oneself.

20.24.1.en: Ben-hadad and his servants, shut up inside the city of Aphek, felt that they were in the hand of the king of Israel and that he would surely seize them and kill them. So in fear Ben-hadad's servants proposed to the king a proposal that might save him and save them with him. They said to him: we know from the history of the kings of the children of Israel that they are forgiving and kind, so we propose that all of us put sackcloth on our loins as a sign of our humbling ourselves before King Ahab, and tie ropes on our heads as a declaration that we deserve to die by hanging with these ropes, and that we beg the king, that he may forgive you and let you live, and so we shall live with you. For Ben-hadad's servants knew from the history of the children of Israel the forgiveness of King Saul toward Agag (1 Sam 15:9) and the forgiveness of David toward Saul and toward Absalom his son.

20.25.0.en: Ben-hadad agreed to his servants' proposal, so they girded on the sackcloth and the ropes and went to King Ahab and begged him to forgive Ben-hadad their king. Ahab marveled that he was still alive, and when he made sure of that he declared his pardon of him, and even said respectfully, "He is my brother", that is, a king of standing like me.

20.25.1.en: Ahab's pardon may seem a kind of mercy and magnanimity, but it was very wrong, for the following reasons:

20.25.2.en: 1- Because it was against God's commandments to destroy the wicked; for he had blasphemed the name of God and said that He was a God of the hills and not a God of the valleys. And Ahab did not take warning from what Saul did when he spared Agag, and God rebuked him by the mouth of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam 15:19).

20.25.3.en: 2- Perhaps the humiliation Ahab tasted before Ben-hadad's threats, before fighting him, found in this situation an opportunity to regain his dignity at the expense of God's word and to forgive his opponent.

20.25.4.en: 3- He made a covenant with Ben-hadad and broke his covenant with God, because he still believed in idol worship such as Baal and did not submit to God, the only God.

20.25.5.en: 4- He did not seek God's counsel, nor did he ask the prophet who had given him the good news what to do with Ben-hadad.

20.25.6.en: 5- His action was against his people. He thought he was being merciful to Ben-hadad, but he was unmerciful to his people, whom Ben-hadad had humiliated and who would return after three years to fight them; so he wronged his people.

20.25.7.en: 6- He did not rebuke Ben-hadad for his blasphemy against God, nor that the cause of his defeat was his defying God, and he did not benefit from the situation by taking compensation for the war losses that Ben-hadad had caused, but was content with Ben-hadad's promise to return to him afterward the cities that his father had taken from Omri, Ahab's father, and to allow him to trade in Damascus.

20.25.8.en: 7- Perhaps he thought that sparing Ben-hadad would make him ally with him against Assyria, which was beginning to grow strong as a state to dominate the world. And he did not rely on God, who protects him.

20.25.9.en: 8- Ahab pretended mercy, but his heart was wicked, for he did not believe in God who gave him victory, did not obey His word, and did not thank Him in any way, and by this he angered God greatly, because God searches the hearts and reins and does not care for appearances.

20.25.10.en: Be merciful to the weak, but do not pretend mercy for purposes in your heart. Do mercy for God's sake and not for any personal purpose, or to please people.

20.26.0.en: They pressed: from persistence, that is, they pressed.

20.26.1.en: Whether it were his: Ben-hadad's servants asked one another whether Ahab truly meant these words, that Ben-hadad was his brother.

20.26.2.en: Ben-hadad's servants were gladdened and rejoiced greatly when they heard Ahab's words that Ben-hadad was his brother, that is, that he had pardoned him. So they caught this word from him and confirmed it, saying to Ahab: "Thy brother Ben-hadad", relying on the fact that kings do not go back on their word. And of course this pardon would include Ben-hadad's servants standing before Ahab, so their joy was great that they would not die.

20.26.3.en: And Ahab commanded that they bring Ben-hadad to him, that is, take him from the city of Aphek and bring him to Ahab. When he came to him, Ahab greeted him and took him by the hand and caused him to come up into his royal chariot, that is, he gave him the honor due to a king.

20.27.0.en: In the face of this great pardon from Ahab and the excessive honor, Ben-hadad declared that he would restore the cities which his father, who was also called Ben-hadad (ch. 15:18), had taken from Omri, Ahab's father, and that he would allow the Jews to trade in Damascus, which was a great commercial city and the capital of Aram. This may imply that they would build houses and quarters for themselves in Damascus, called the quarters of the Jews, to establish their trade.

20.27.1.en: Ahab rejoiced at these promises and made a covenant with Ben-hadad, since he thought this was to the benefit of the Jews, as we mentioned at (v. 32).

20.28.0.en: After Elijah killed the prophets of Baal, Jezebel grew weaker to some extent, so the sons of the prophets began to appear, who gather in the schools of the prophets that the prophet Samuel founded, and one of the most important rules of these schools was obedience to God. So one of these prophets came forward and said to another prophet, his companion, that God commanded him to strike him. But the prophet's friend was ashamed, or took pity on his fellow prophet who was commanding him from God to strike him, and refused to obey God's word and strike the prophet.

20.29.0.en: When this friend refused to obey God's command, the prophet told him a message from God, that because he refused to obey God, when he left the place where he was and went on his way a lion would meet him and kill him, and this actually happened.

20.29.1.en: All this is so that God may confirm to us the importance of obedience, because Ahab's sin in sparing Ben-hadad was refusing to obey God.

20.30.0.en: This prophet continued on his way and met another man and asked him the same request that God wanted, which was that he strike him. When the man learned that this was a command from God, he obeyed and struck him hard until he wounded him, and this is what the prophet wanted, that signs should appear on him showing that he was a soldier who had been struck and wounded in the war.

20.31.0.en: Bandage: a long piece of cloth tied on the head over the cap or tied on wounds.

20.31.1.en: The prophet bound the wound on his head with a large bandage, so that it covered most of his eyes and therefore concealed to a great extent the features of his face, so that Ahab would not know that he was a prophet, because he fears the prophets, since they represent God and make him hear His voice rebuking him for his mistakes. Then he waited for King Ahab on his return from Aphek, after he had bidden farewell to King Ben-hadad king of Aram, to make him hear a message from God.

20.32.0.en: After a while the king reached the place where the prophet was, and the prophet called out to him, asking for his guidance and judgment. The king stopped with his chariot and the disguised prophet came forward, as if he were a soldier wounded in the war, and told the king that when he was in the battle, one man, probably a commander, came to him and asked him to keep a certain prisoner with all care and attention, and threatened him that if he did not keep him or he got lost, he would be seized in his place, or would pay a large sum of money, a talent of silver, which equals about three thousand shekels. And the price of a slave, as we know from the sale of Christ by Judas, is thirty pieces of silver, that is, this prisoner was very important and his price a hundred times that of an ordinary slave. The prophet intended by this story, to which God guided him, to alert the king so that he would understand the truth of what he had done, since he had released a very precious prisoner, Ben-hadad, but the king did not understand the meaning of the parable.

20.32.1.en: Then the prophet continued his speech and said that during the battle he moved right and left and was not careful in guarding the prisoner, so he escaped from him; that is, he was busy with the business of war, but the result was the loss of the prisoner. Then he asked the king's judgment, perhaps to rescue him from this predicament, but the king in all harshness said to him: you have judged yourself by your promise and agreement to keep this prisoner, so you must be seized in his place.

20.33.0.en: After the prophet told the king this story, he lifted the bandage that was on his head and covered his eyes, and the mark that the prophets used to put on their foreheads, declaring their identity, appeared, so that people would know them and accept God's word from their mouths. And here Ahab discovered that he was one of the prophets, and he was afraid, since he expected a message from God, because he was wicked and greatly angered God.

20.34.0.en: The prophet declared God's message plainly to Ahab and rebuked him for releasing the wicked Ben-hadad, who had blasphemed God and whom God in His Law had commanded to be killed, so Ahab deserved to have done to him what ought to have been done to Ben-hadad, that is, to die. And here only Ahab understood the meaning of the parable; indeed perhaps the prophet told him what had happened to his companion who did not obey God's command and was killed by the lion, so Ahab understood that since he had not obeyed God's word he deserved death.

20.34.1.en: And the message carried not only punishment of death for Ahab, but also that his people would die in place of Aram, because the people also shared in the fault with Ahab in the worship of Baal and had not returned with all their hearts to God.

20.35.0.en: When Ahab heard God's judgment by the mouth of the prophet, he was very sad and went on his way to his house in Samaria, the capital of his kingdom, but he did not return to God by repentance, because his heart was far from God, although before him was a practical example, namely Ben-hadad's seeking Ahab's mercy and Ahab's forgiving him (v. 31). How much more, then, will the tender God forgive His children if they take refuge in Him, and as He forgave the great David for his fault.

20.35.1.en: Beware of the sorrow without hope, which is sorrow over what you lose of the things of this world. And if you meet any trouble, or err in any matter, take refuge in God, confident of His mercies and forgiveness.
